q: Construct the classic pairing logic for white truffle risotto.
accept: aged nebbiolo barolo mature aromatics no oak power echo
mature barolo barbaresco aged champagne
ans: Mature Nebbiolo (or aged Champagne): tertiary aromatics echo truffle; structure stays out of the way — never young oak or heavy fruit
exp: Truffle is aroma, not weight: pair to the nose.

q: Kaiseki's pairing challenge and the somm's frame:
accept: many small courses umami subtlety sake and delicate wines progression
one beverage arc restraint sake champagne riesling
ans: A dozen subtle umami courses defeat bottle-per-course logic — build a restrained arc (sake, Champagne, mature Riesling) that never overtakes the kitchen
exp: Sometimes mastery is choosing less wine.

q: Why do tannic reds fail with blue cheese where sweet wines succeed — the receptor-level answer?
accept: umami glutamate piquancy amplify bitterness sugar and acid buffer
salt piquancy amplify bitterness sugar and acid buffer
capsaicin-like piquance tannin clash sugar rescue
ans: Blue's glutamate-rich umami and piquancy amplify tannin's bitterness and astringency; sugar-acid pairs buffer and flatter instead
exp: Then name Stilton-Port's exception: tawny's resolved tannin and sweetness thread the needle.

accept: add element to dish echoing wine
garnish links dish and wine mushrooms herbs citrus
ans: Adjusting the plate — a citrus, herb, or earth element — to meet the wine halfway (somm-kitchen collaboration)
exp: MS pairing questions reward two-way thinking: the dish can move too.

q: Menu wines for a strict-vegan tasting menu: name the structural challenge and two safe archetypes.
accept: no animal fat lighter proteins high acid whites low tannin reds fining vegan
umami vegetables acid-driven wines unfined
ans: Without animal fat/protein, tannin has nothing to bind — favor acid-driven whites, skin-contact texture, low-tannin chillable reds; verify vegan fining
exp: Chemistry first, certification second — both get asked.

q: Pair the last course: 85% dark chocolate torte. Defend one choice against one rejected alternative.
accept: banyuls maury tawny vs cabernet sauternes rejected
vintage-character fortified over dry red or lighter sweet
ans: Banyuls/Maury (or aged Tawny): cocoa-echoing rancio, sugar above the torte's, soft grip — over dry Cabernet (tannin war) or Sauternes (botrytis honey and stone fruit fight cocoa, and its delicacy is buried by 85%)
exp: State the two laws you're obeying: sweeter-than, and echo-don't-fight.

q: Explain 'the third flavor' concept in pairing.
accept: wine and food create new flavor neither has alone
synergy creating something new
ans: A great pairing produces a flavor neither element holds alone — synergy, not mere compatibility
exp: Sauternes and Roquefort make caramel neither possesses; that is the target.

q: Build a pairing argument for oysters and mature Champagne against the classic Muscadet.
accept: autolytic brioche echoes brine acidity texture versus simple freshness
champagne complexity versus muscadet purity
ans: Mature Champagne brings autolytic brioche and oxidative depth to echo the oyster's mineral-cream finish, with mousse scrubbing texture; Muscadet offers purity and salt without complexity — choose by the oyster's richness
exp: Master answers argue both sides and then commit.

q: Pair a full tasting menu's cheese and dessert transition without exhausting the guest. Explain the arc.
accept: smaller pours fortified or sweet white bridge lower alcohol
transition with a bridging wine
~bridging wine
~one wine that serves both
ans: Bridge with one wine that serves both — an aged Tawny, an off-dry Vouvray or a Sherry — in a small pour, rather than a separate glass for each; the palate is tired and the alcohol budget is spent
exp: Restraint is a pairing skill at the end of a menu.

q: A guest orders a mature Bordeaux with a heavily spiced dish. How do you handle it?
accept: serve it advise sequencing offer intermediate glass do not lecture
serve and manage gracefully
ans: Serve it. Offer to pour it with the courses that suit and suggest a glass alongside for the spiced dish — manage the sequence rather than the guest's choice
exp: The hospitality answer beats the theoretical one every time.

q: Design a pairing for a vegetarian umami-forward dish — mushroom, miso, aged cheese — and justify it.
accept: aged champagne junmai sake oxidative jura or sherry no tannin
umami-tolerant wines
ans: Aged Champagne, junmai sake, oxidative Jura or Amontillado — wines with umami of their own and no tannin to be hardened by glutamates
exp: Never send a young tannic red into an umami dish.

q: Distinguish congruent from complementary pairing. Give an example of each and name the failure mode each carries.
accept: congruent echoes shared flavours and can turn monotonous while complementary contrasts them and one side can dominate
echo pairing versus contrast pairing with monotony or domination as the failures
congruent shares compounds and risks excess contrast balances and risks one side winning
similarity pairing versus counterpoint pairing each with its own failure mode
ans: Congruent pairing shares flavour compounds or characters and amplifies what both already hold — smoked brisket with a toasty Syrah, mature Nebbiolo with white truffle, brioche-scented Champagne with fried food. Its failure mode is monotony and excess: two loud voices saying the same word, with nothing left to refresh the palate. Complementary or contrast pairing sets one element against another — Sauternes against Roquefort, brut Champagne against salt and fat, Riesling's sugar against chilli heat. Its failure mode is domination: one side simply wins, the dish erased by the wine or the wine flattened by the dish. The best pairings usually run both axes at once — contrast in structure, echo in aroma — and a Master answer names which axis it is using and why.
exp: Most candidates can produce good pairings and cannot say why they are good. Naming the axis converts a lucky answer into a method — and the failure modes are the part examiners listen for, because they show you know what your own choice risks.

q: Assess 'what grows together goes together' as doctrine. Argue for it, then argue against it.
accept: co-evolution makes it usually work but it is correlation not chemistry
regional logic is a good default that fails for modern menus and wineless cuisines
argue tradition and structural fit then argue it is not a mechanism
yes for classic regional dishes no for cuisines that never had wine
ans: For: regional cuisine and regional wine co-evolved over centuries of mutual selection, so the structural fit is usually real — Muscadet with Loire oysters, Chianti's acid against tomato, Alsace Riesling with charcuterie, Fino with the tapas that were built to be eaten beside it. It is also the fastest reliable default under service pressure, and it gives the guest a story that makes the pairing land. Against: it is correlation wearing the coat of chemistry. Many regions historically drank whatever was to hand and shipped the good bottles away; modern kitchens plate almost nothing their grandparents ate; grape plantings have moved; and the heuristic falls silent for every cuisine with no wine tradition at all, where sake, Sherry and aromatic whites are found by structure alone. Use it to build the shortlist, never to close the argument.
exp: Examiners use this prompt to see whether you can hold a heuristic and its limits at the same time. A candidate who defends the maxim absolutely, or dismisses it as folklore, has failed the question either way — the answer is that it is a good prior and a bad proof.

q: One wine must be poured for two hundred guests choosing among three main courses. Name the structural profile you look for, two wines that fit, and what you refuse.
accept: moderate alcohol high acid low oak low tannin crowd wine like cru beaujolais
fresh mid-weight fruit-forward wines with no big oak or high alcohol
acid-driven flexible wines beaujolais cabernet franc unoaked chardonnay
choose flexibility over power and refuse oaky high-alcohol reds
ans: Look for moderate alcohol, genuine freshness, fine-grained or absent tannin, little to no new oak, and generous fruit without sweetness — a wine that flatters rather than argues, and that will survive being poured early and standing warm on a table. Reds: Cru Beaujolais, mid-weight Loire Cabernet Franc, Barbera d'Alba, a good Côtes du Rhône Villages. Whites: dry Chenin, unoaked Chardonnay, Grüner Veltliner, dry Furmint. Refuse the wines whose virtues are also their risks: high-alcohol oaked Cabernet or Shiraz, young tannic Barolo, anything reductive or botrytised, anything needing decanting on a schedule or a narrow serving window, and anything so distinctive that a third of the room will dislike it. The constraint here is service as much as chemistry — banquet pairing is the art of choosing flexibility over brilliance.
exp: Every restaurant pairing question assumes ideal service; the banquet question removes it. The wine will be opened an hour early, poured at whatever temperature the room is, and drunk with three different plates — so the answer is a profile, not a bottle, and the reasoning has to include logistics.

q: Distinguish aromatic spice from piquant heat in pairing terms, and give the wine logic for each.
accept: capsaicin is pain needing low alcohol and sugar while aromatic spice is an aroma match
heat versus perfume one is structural the other aromatic
trpv1 heat wants sweetness and low alcohol while aromatic spice wants terpene whites
off-dry aromatic whites solve both because sugar answers heat and aroma answers spice
ans: Piquant heat is capsaicin, or piperine in pepper, acting on the TRPV1 pain receptor. Ethanol activates the same receptor and tannin sharpens the burn, so the answer is structural: low alcohol, low tannin, cold service, and residual sugar to blanket the heat — Kabinett Riesling, Moscato d'Asti, off-dry Vouvray. Aromatic spice — cardamom, cumin, coriander, star anise, saffron, ras el hanout — is not pain at all but perfume, and it is an aroma-matching problem: terpene-driven aromatic whites such as Gewürztraminer, Muscat or Torrontés, or spice-toned reds such as Grenache, Cinsault, or Syrah with its own peppery rotundone. Most Indian, Thai and North African cooking is both at once, which is precisely why an off-dry aromatic white solves so much of it: the sugar answers the heat while the terpenes answer the perfume.
exp: 'Spicy food' is two unrelated problems that happen to share an English word, and candidates who treat them as one give the sugar answer to a dish that has no chilli in it. Separate the pain receptor from the nose, then say which one the dish in front of you actually poses.

accept: young wine resting classified before solera entry
holding stage after fortification before criaderas
ans: The classified young wine's resting stage (fortified, marked una raya or dos rayas at the first classification) before entering the youngest criadera
exp: First classification decides 15% flor track or 17%+ oxidative track.
